title: Looking Back in Time
paragraphs: The James Webb Space Telescope was launched on Christmas Day in two thousand twenty one, and astronomers have been using it to study the early universe ever since. After launch, it travelled for about a month to reach a region roughly one and a half million kilometres from Earth. Near that point, the gravity of the Sun and Earth combine in a way that lets a spacecraft hold a steady position.

Unlike the Hubble telescope, which mostly observes visible light, Webb is an infrared observatory. Its main mirror is about six and a half metres wide, and it is built from eighteen hexagonal segments coated with a thin layer of gold. The segments are aligned so precisely that they behave like a single giant mirror. This design lets the mirror collect a great deal of faint light.

Light takes time to travel, so the light from faraway galaxies left them long ago. Studying that light is therefore a form of looking into the past. Many of these objects are far too faint for older telescopes. Webb's infrared sensitivity lets astronomers observe some of the earliest galaxies that have been detected.
